entries.title: Man charged in fatal late-night Lake View beating
entries.summary: <p>A man has been charged in the fatal beating of another man in Lake View, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Mateusz Mysliwiec, 35, was arrested Sunday on a charge of first-degree murder, police said.</p><p>Mysliwiec is alleged to have killed a 51-year-old man in the 800 block of West Wellington Avenue just before midnight on Oct. 2, police said.</p><p>He is due in court again Wednesday.</p>

entries.title: Former CPS employees plead guilty to federal fraud charges in district contract kickback scheme
entries.summary: <p>A former Chicago Public Schools principal and an ex-CPS employee plead guilty to fraud in federal court for their roles in a kickback scheme that took thousands from local school districts, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Illinois.</p><p>Antonio Ross and Alfonzo Lewis both signed plea deals Tuesday after being <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/10/09/ex-superintendent-of-evanston-skokie-school-district-65-at-center-of-federal-corruption-indictment" target="_blank" ><u>indicted</u></a><u> </u>just over a year ago, according to court records.</p><p>The two allegedly created companies to apply as vendors for professional service contracts with District 65, submitting “false and fraudulent” documents to win them and then hid thousands of dollars in kickbacks to then-district superintendent Devon Horton, according to prosecutors.</p><p>Ross, then serving as Hyde Park Academy High School principal, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/10/09/ex-superintendent-of-evanston-skokie-school-district-65-at-center-of-federal-corruption-indictment" target="_blank" ><u>obtained nearly $120,000 from District 65</u></a> and paid Horton nearly $42,000 from the proceeds, prosecutors said. </p><p>The scheme ran from August 2020 to June 2023, court documents said. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5d0000" name="image-5d0000"></a> allegedly received $24,000 from the district — about a quarter of which he gave to Horton. Both admitted their companies didn’t perform some services they were paid for. </p><p>Lewis, according to a CPS spokesperson, had been suspended pending the outcome of the federal investigation. </p><p>In addition to the kickback scheme with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/05/02/u-s-department-of-education-investigating-evanston-skokie-schools-racial-discrimination" target="_blank" ><u>District 65</u></a>, Ross awarded Horton’s company a service contract with CPS and approved $10,000 in false invoices for services by Horton’s company that were never completed, according to court documents.</p><p>Ross was dismissed by CPS in 2023 for “engaging in public benefits fraud by deliberately obtaining a federal <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/ppp-paycheck-protection-program-covid-relief" target="_blank" ><u>Paycheck Protection Program</u></a> loan and PPP loan forgiveness through fraudulent means,” according to his dismissal proceedings in front of a state board hearing officer.</p><p>Horton, previously a superintendent of the DeKalb County School District in Georgia, was placed on administrative leave last fall, according to a statement on the district’s website. He pleaded guilty to wire fraud, embezzlement, and tax charges earlier this month, according to prosecutors. </p><p>In January, he was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/02/02/devon-horton-evanston-skokie-school-district-assault-charge" target="_blank" ><u>arrested and charged</u></a> on a felony count of aggravated assault, strangulation and a misdemeanor count of cruelty to children in the third degree.</p><p>District 65 didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/10/09/ex-superintendent-of-evanston-skokie-school-district-65-at-center-of-federal-corruption-indictment" >Ex-superintendent of Evanston/Skokie School District 65 at center of federal corruption indictment</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Chicago Park District said Griffin MSI's planned Welcome Hall is too big before supporting project anyway
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Park District asked the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry to shrink the size of the 458-foot long, two-story Welcome Hall that's planned for the institution’s main entry — but later supported the design after consulting with preservationists in the government and local nonprofit fields.</p><p>The Welcome Hall, which would be located outside the historic building’s North Portico, “quickly rises to a height that visually blocks the lower portions of the historic facades from most vantage points beyond the corners of the original courtyard,” Chicago Park District Planning and Research Manager Nelson Chueng wrote in a March 24 letter to Griffin MSI's Vice President of Government Affairs Anne Rashford.</p><p>Chueng also said the new structure would be “entirely modern, in stark contrast to the [museum’s] strict Beaux-Arts design,” and asked if there were any earlier schemes for the hall “that continued the classical expression and related directly to the historic building facades.”</p><p>The points raised in the letter echo much of the public criticism that has been leveled at the museum and its architects, RAMSA, since renderings of the project were released last month.</p><p>I've <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/09/24/griffin-msi-carbuncle-done-deal-chicago-park-district" >criticized the structure’s look</a>, size and lack of architectural compatibility to the museum’s Greek Revival design.</p><p>The two-page missive was given to me by park district officials Tuesday, following a request I made last week about the document.</p><p>Just a few hours before I received the letter, officials broke ground on a $22 million effort to convert the building’s seldom-used South Portico entrance — located on the other side of the museum from the planned Welcome Hall site — into an accessible full-time entry that would feature a new outdoor terrace, cafe, elevators and lobby space. </p><p>The building was originally the Palace of Fine Arts, built for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/10/11/griffin-msi-construction-22-million-south-portico-renovation" >South Portico</a>, which was the building's main entrance during the fair, hasn't been routinely open to the public for the past 130 years.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ed0000" name="image-ed0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/51a46ac/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F38%2F5e%2Faec2026945c8a60427452806f59f%2Fmsiportico-261013-07.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/07acc5d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F38%2F5e%2Faec2026945c8a60427452806f59f%2Fmsiportico-261013-07.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9a7b081/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F38%2F5e%2Faec2026945c8a60427452806f59f%2Fmsiportico-261013-07.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="State Rep. Curtis J. Tarver II speaks during the Richard H. Driehaus South Portico groundbreaking ceremony." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9a7b081/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F38%2F5e%2Faec2026945c8a60427452806f59f%2Fmsiportico-261013-07.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2f03752/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F38%2F5e%2Faec2026945c8a60427452806f59f%2Fmsiportico-261013-07.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9a7b081/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F38%2F5e%2Faec2026945c8a60427452806f59f%2Fmsiportico-261013-07.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>State Rep. Curtis J. Tarver II speaks during the Richard H. Driehaus South Portico groundbreaking ceremony.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kameron Clepper/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Chicago Park District General Supt. and CEO Carlos Ramirez-Rosa attended the groundbreaking ceremony and made favorable remarks about the South Portico project.</p><p>But afterward, Ramirez-Rosa told me the park district raised concerns last spring about the North Portico Welcome Hall design, as part of the agency’s design review process.</p><p>“Some of them were addressed through the design review process,” he said. </p><p>But the park district decided to back off after receiving letters of support for the project’s design from the preservation group Landmarks Illinois and the state’s historic preservation office, Ramirez-Rosa said.</p><p>“Ultimately, we deferred to the experts and supported the project moving forward through the city’s permitting process,” he said. “We are parks management experts. We are not historic preservation experts.”</p><p>Museum officials didn't publicly mention the North Portico project during the South Portico's groundbreaking. Museum officials previously said both projects are part of efforts to create new, admission-free public spaces and improve accessibility.</p><p>The South Portico — the museum’s largest construction effort since spending $35 million in 2005 to restore the U-505 submarine and build a new shelter for the captured WWII vessel — is expected to be completed in December 2027.</p><div Humphrey said residents told her the closed entrance felt as if the museum had turned its back on the community.</p><p>“That is what was asked for [by the community]: Creating a better experience for our guests and neighbors,” Humphrey said. “We want everyone to feel like they belong here. This is their museum and they can enter this space by saying, ‘This is my museum.’”</p><p>The renovated entrance will be renamed the Richard H. Driehaus Foundation South Portico, in honor of the philanthropic organization started in 1983 by the late Chicago businessman and investor. The foundation donated $10 million toward the portico renovation, which is the largest gift awarded by the organization.</p>

entries.title: There's a lot of movement on the basketball court
entries.summary: <p>New faces heading to new places in Illinois high school basketball has been a growing trend over the last several years.</p><p>As the transfer has become so ho-hum and commonplace in the sport, it’s a challenge to track the total amount of transfers. The number far surpasses 100. But with practice officially starting in just a few weeks, here are several transfers whose impact could be felt the most this upcoming season.</p><p><i>•</i><b> Caden Crudup, Marist (from Young):</b> The defending Class 4A state champs welcome a 6-4 jack-of-all-trades senior veteran. Crudup, who averaged 10 points and eight rebounds as a junior, can be an impactful piece for a team lacking experience.</p><p><i> • </i><b>CJ Pittman, Young (Payton):</b> A steady, playmaking point guard with scoring ability switches high-academic city schools. Pittman averaged 18 points and six assists as a sophomore a year ago.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Dakari Nesbitt, Thornwood (Thornton):</b> The sophomore guard made an immediate presence last season, putting up nearly 15 points per game. He now joins a talented backcourt featuring Lester Watson and Mekhi Young.</p><p><i>• </i><b>DK Heard, King (Mount Carmel):</b> The most noteworthy local transfer. The physically gifted Heard left Mount Carmel last month. The 6-4 guard is one of the top-ranked players in the Class of 2029 after opening eyes as a freshman a year ago.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Donavyn Simmons, Romeoville (Joliet Catholic): </b>Simmons instantly becomes one of the top players in the Southwest Prairie Conference. The 6-2 combo guard has quietly been one of the bigger producers in the senior class, averaging 12.4 points as a sophomore and 15 points last season.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Elijah and Malachi Bell, Marian Central (Jacobs): </b>The brothers join their father, Lafayette Bell, who is the new coach at Marian. Senior Elijah Bell filled the stat sheet last season at Jacobs with 16 points, five rebounds and a couple of steals and assists a game. Sophomore Malachi Bell will make another jump after putting up 10 points per game.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Jacob Only, DePaul Prep (St. Viator):</b> Look for a breakout season from the smooth, long and rangy 6-3 guard after showing so much upside as a sophomore when he averaged 13 points and three assists.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Jayden and Tray Alford, Oswego (Yorkville Christian): </b>A team already returning several starters from a 22-win season welcomes the Alford brothers back to Oswego. Senior Tray Alford surpassed 1,000 career points at Yorkville Christian, while Jayden Alford is a promising 6-1 sophomore guard.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Lameck Hassan, Romeoville (Danville Christian, Ky.):</b> This is a big wild card in several ways. Hassan is a young, raw player in the junior class who moved in from Kentucky. But there is no denying his upside and potential impact at 6-10.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Mikey Woods, Perspectives-Leadership (Don Bosco Prep, Ind.):</b> Arguably the biggest arrival for any program, the talented guard began his high school career as an impressive freshman at De Sales. The dangerous downhill guard’s impact will be felt immediately.</p><p><i>• </i><b>Nate Woods, Bolingbrook (Lyons):</b> The addition of one of the better perimeter shooters in the senior class will be a boon for what will be another highly ranked Bolingbrook team. The 6-6 Woods played a big part for Lyons' 23-win team a year ago.</p>

entries.title: Bears' Caleb Williams, Colston Loveland turn up for premiere of 'Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story'
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> tight end Colston Loveland is used to getting yelled at by coach Ben Johnson, but the crew of Hallmark’s “Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story,” was even more demanding about the details.</p><p>Loveland has a cameo in the movie, which premiered Tuesday in Lake Forest and will debut Saturday on Hallmark Channel, and the job was tougher than he expected.</p><p>“I was moving around too much sometimes and messing up the shot,” he said, alluding to some nerves about his acting debut. “I’d move my shoulder an inch and they’d say, ‘Make sure you stand still.’ That was new.”</p><p>Several others from the organization attended the premiere at Gorton Center, including president Kevin Warren, general manager Ryan Poles and quarterback Caleb Williams.</p><p>Williams’ hamstring was in good enough shape to walk the red carpet, but the Bears still don’t know whether he’ll be available for their game Sunday at the Falcons. Williams posed for photos, did a video for the team in which he said it was “pretty cool” for the Bears to be featured in a Hallmark movie and left.</p><p>Getting him on board for a cameo was massive for Hallmark. The Bears are the third team to do a “Holiday Touchdown” movie, following the Chiefs in 2024 and the Bills last season, and the company wasn’t able to get Patrick Mahomes or Josh Allen for those films.</p><p>“For me, he was the No. 1 get, [but] he’s busy and with Madden and everything, his summer was pandemonium,” director Dustin Rikert said. “But he came through, and it was a real thrill.”</p><p>Like Williams, Rikert went to USC, and Williams greeted him on the red carpet with, “Fight on.”</p><p>Rikert didn’t want to spoil any surprises about the cameos, but when asked which of the non-actors from the Bears was the most natural on set, the first thing he said was, “Cole Kmet is hilarious in this.”</p><p>Loveland might want to pay attention.</p><p>He had a scene with actress Barbara Alyn Woods in which they were directed mostly to improvise, and Woods had to coach him into character.</p><p>“I feel like I drew him out a little bit,” she said. “He was being a little bit timid. I said, ‘Do what you would do in this situation,’ and then he kind of went for it. Every time, he got it a little bit more.”</p><p>Woods jumped at the chance to be in a movie set in Chicago. She grew up in Darien and went to Hinsdale South High School and Northern Illinois and has been a lifelong Bears fan. Her only complaint was that they filmed in July, and since the story is Christmas-themed, the cast wore winter gear during the blistering summer heat.</p><p>Also, she was quite displeased with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/11/bears-coach-ben-johnson-runs-out-of-answers-unable-to-ignite-offense-in-31-7-loss-to-packers" >the Bears’ 31-7 loss to the Packers at Lambeau Field</a> on Sunday.</p><p>“It sucks,” she said. “That’s going to be the only loss. This movie is going to give them confidence in such a big way that they’re never going to lose again.”</p><p>Only a master thespian like her could make that sound believable.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/10/13/chicago-bears-edition-of-hallmarks-holiday-touchdown-is-a-gooey-homage-to-the-city" >Chicago Bears edition of Hallmark’s ‘Holiday Touchdown’ is a gooey homage to the city</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: 12-year-old grazed by bullet in Near West Side park
entries.summary: <p>A 12-year-old was grazed by a bullet while playing in a Near West Side park Tuesday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The boy was in Starr Park in the 2200 block of West Maypole Avenue at 5:10 p.m. when he was grazed in his thigh by a bullet, police said. He was taken to Stroger Hospital in good condition.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said. An investigation is ongoing.</p>
